title: Metabolic-bioactivation structural alerts
framing: LIABILITY FLAG ONLY. A match means this substructure has been associated with reactive-metabolite formation in the medicinal-chemistry literature. It is NOT a statement that the compound is toxic, and it is not a prediction that bioactivation occurs: whether it does depends on the enzymes present, the competing clearance routes, the dose and the detoxication capacity, none of which a substructure knows. Marketed, widely used drugs match several of these alerts.
notice: PAINS (Baell & Holloway), Brenk, and the ChEMBL-derived Glaxo/Dundee/BMS/Inpharmatica/SureChEMBL alert sets are DELIBERATELY NOT bundled in this pack. Those SMARTS collections are redistributed under BSD-3 (RDKit FilterCatalog data) and CC BY-SA 3.0 (ChEMBL-derived sets); shipping them inside an Apache-2.0 product requires a separately-licensed pack plus a NOTICE entry, and getting that attribution wrong is a real legal problem rather than a cosmetic one. If those sets are wanted later they belong in their own pack file carrying their own licence header. The alerts below are authored in-house from the metabolic-bioactivation literature, where no machine-readable SMARTS set exists to copy in the first place.
conceptSource: Stepan AF, Walker DP, Bauman J, Price DA, Baillie TA, Kalgutkar AS, Aleo MD. Structural alert/reactive metabolite concept as applied in medicinal chemistry to mitigate the risk of idiosyncratic drug toxicity: a perspective based on the critical examination of trends in the top 200 drugs marketed in the United States. Chem Res Toxicol. 2011;24(9):1345-1410. doi:10.1021/tx200168d

alerts.label: para-Aminophenol / anilide (quinone-imine former)
alerts.mechanism: CYP oxidation of the 4-aminophenol motif gives a quinone imine (the acetaminophen/NAPQI case), an electrophile trapped by glutathione and by protein thiols once glutathione is depleted.
alerts.citation: Stepan et al. 2011, Chem Res Toxicol 24:1345-1410, doi:10.1021/tx200168d

alerts.label: para-Alkoxyaniline (quinone-imine former after O-dealkylation)
alerts.mechanism: O-dealkylation unmasks a para-aminophenol, which is then oxidised to a quinone imine; this is the phenacetin route to the same electrophile as acetaminophen.
alerts.citation: Stepan et al. 2011, Chem Res Toxicol 24:1345-1410, doi:10.1021/tx200168d

alerts.label: Catechol (ortho-dihydroxyarene, quinone former)
alerts.mechanism: Two-electron oxidation gives an ortho-quinone that redox-cycles and alkylates thiols; the same motif is also the COMT substrate that dominates catecholamine clearance.
alerts.citation: Stepan et al. 2011, Chem Res Toxicol 24:1345-1410, doi:10.1021/tx200168d

alerts.label: Hydroquinone (para-dihydroxyarene, quinone former)
alerts.mechanism: Oxidation gives a para-quinone; like the catechol it redox-cycles, producing both an electrophile and oxidative stress.
alerts.citation: Stepan et al. 2011, Chem Res Toxicol 24:1345-1410, doi:10.1021/tx200168d

alerts.label: Nitroaromatic
alerts.mechanism: Nitroreduction proceeds through nitroso and N-hydroxylamine intermediates that bind protein and can redox-cycle; gut-flora and mammalian nitroreductases both do it.
alerts.citation: Stepan et al. 2011, Chem Res Toxicol 24:1345-1410, doi:10.1021/tx200168d

alerts.label: Primary aromatic amine (aniline)
alerts.mechanism: N-oxidation gives hydroxylamine and nitroso species; ring oxidation of the corresponding aminophenol gives a quinone imine. Both electrophiles are protein-reactive.
alerts.citation: Stepan et al. 2011, Chem Res Toxicol 24:1345-1410, doi:10.1021/tx200168d

alerts.label: Thiophene
alerts.mechanism: CYP oxidation gives an S-oxide or a thiophene epoxide, both Michael-type electrophiles. Many marketed drugs carry this ring, so the flag records a route, not an outcome.
alerts.citation: Stepan et al. 2011, Chem Res Toxicol 24:1345-1410, doi:10.1021/tx200168d

alerts.label: Furan
alerts.mechanism: CYP oxidation gives an epoxide that opens to a reactive cis-enedione, which cross-links protein nucleophiles.
alerts.citation: Stepan et al. 2011, Chem Res Toxicol 24:1345-1410, doi:10.1021/tx200168d

alerts.label: Terminal alkyne
alerts.mechanism: CYP oxidation of the terminal carbon gives a ketene or an oxirene that acylates the enzyme, which is the classic mechanism-based CYP inactivation motif.
alerts.citation: Stepan et al. 2011, Chem Res Toxicol 24:1345-1410, doi:10.1021/tx200168d

alerts.label: Hydrazine / hydrazide (N-N single bond)
alerts.mechanism: Oxidative N-N cleavage gives diazenes and carbon-centred radicals; the acetylhydrazine route from isoniazid is the reference case.
alerts.citation: Stepan et al. 2011, Chem Res Toxicol 24:1345-1410, doi:10.1021/tx200168d

alerts.label: Epoxide (already electrophilic)
alerts.mechanism: A strained oxirane alkylates thiol and amine nucleophiles directly; no metabolic activation is required, only failure of epoxide hydrolase and glutathione to intercept it.
alerts.citation: Stepan et al. 2011, Chem Res Toxicol 24:1345-1410, doi:10.1021/tx200168d

alerts.label: Michael acceptor (alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl)
alerts.mechanism: The beta carbon is attacked directly by glutathione and by protein cysteines; this is intrinsic reactivity, not bioactivation, and it is also how covalent inhibitors are designed on purpose.
alerts.citation: Stepan et al. 2011, Chem Res Toxicol 24:1345-1410, doi:10.1021/tx200168d

alerts.label: Carboxylic acid on a lipophilic scaffold (acyl glucuronide precursor)
alerts.mechanism: Glucuronidation of the acid gives an acyl glucuronide that transacylates and glycates protein; the 1-O-acyl migration rate, and therefore the liability, rises with scaffold lipophilicity and alpha-substitution.
alerts.citation: Stepan et al. 2011, Chem Res Toxicol 24:1345-1410, doi:10.1021/tx200168d

alerts.label: Thiourea / thioamide
alerts.mechanism: Flavin monooxygenase and CYP S-oxidation give sulfenic and sulfinic acids that oxidise and cross-link protein thiols.
alerts.citation: Stepan et al. 2011, Chem Res Toxicol 24:1345-1410, doi:10.1021/tx200168d

alerts.label: alpha-Haloamide
alerts.mechanism: The activated carbon is displaced by thiols directly, so the amide alkylates glutathione and protein cysteines without any enzymatic step.
alerts.citation: Stepan et al. 2011, Chem Res Toxicol 24:1345-1410, doi:10.1021/tx200168d
